newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar content to stay out of limelight.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar content to stay out of limelight.

text.p: The Australian dollar was left on the trading sidelines as market attention was focused on the regional reaction to the U.S. stockmarket fall on Friday.
The local dollar traded a rough 20 point range through the morning, bouncing off the US$0.7400/10 support area a number of times but lacking the momentum to break above US$0.7420/30.
Although the local stock market weakened, there was little currency selling seen related to the stocks fall.
By noon (0200 GMT) the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7424/29, up from an early US$0.7415/25 but still down on its local Friday close of US$0.7430/35.

Most regional attention was focused on stock markets after the U.S Dow Jones index fell by 247.37 points, or 3.11 percent, on Friday. This was the index's second largest one day points drop, exceeded only by the October 1987 crash.

In early trading the Australian stock exchange fell by 76.4 points or 2.9 percent to a low of 2589.8, but recovered by noon to be above 2,600. At noon, the All Ordinaries Index stood at 2619.0, down 47.2 points or 1.8 percent from Friday's close.
The Nikkei 225 Index also fell by more than two percent in early trade, before recovering some ground. By noon it was down 374.23 points, or 1.94 percent, at 18,951.80.

For its part, the dollar was largely unaffected through the morning, and there was little on the horizon that was seen having the potential to shake it out of the broad US$0.73-$0.75 trading band it has been in since the beginning of July.

While expectations of a sixth rate cut are seen capping the dollar, some improvement in commodity prices over recent weeks, domestic bond market fundamentals and the recent turmoil in some Asian currencies are supportive of the dollar, analysts said.
The buying seen last week from about 74 U.S. cents, some of which was seen again this morning, was also seen putting a floor under the dollar.
Treasury Secretary Ted Evans appeared before a parliamentary committee this morning, and was quite upbeat on the outlook for the economy.
Evans said that official forecasts for inflation were conservative, and that June quarter economic growth data due in early September would show stronger growth than in 1996.
The fall in the Australian dollar from a peak of just above US$0.8000 in March was also a positive for growth, he said.
"The exchange rate change, we believe, will be quite significant in terms of consolidating that forecast of four percent growth in the non-farm sector," Evans said.
While trading was quiet against the U.S. dollar, the Australian dollar was a bit more lively on the crosses -- mainly because of the fall in the U.S. dollar on Friday and in early Asian trade.
The Australian dollar was trading at 87.03/13 yen and 1.3426/43 marks from an early 86.80/90 yen and 1.3453/75 marks, and down from Friday's late 87.86/96 and 1.3697/14.
